content: The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index (PCEPI), also referred to as the PCE deflator, PCE price deflator, Implicit Price Deflator for Personal Consumption Expenditures (IPD for PCE) by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), or the chain-type price index for personal consumption expenditures (CTPIPCE) by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), is a comprehensive measure of the average increase in prices for all domestic personal consumption within the United States. This index is benchmarked to a base value of 100 as of 1992. Unlike the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the Producer Price Index (PPI), the PCEPI is derived from the largest component of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as reported in the BEA's National Income and Product Accounts, specifically personal consumption expenditures. A less volatile version of the PCEPI is the core PCE price index, which excludes the more variable and seasonally influenced prices of food and energy. In contrast to the headline U.S. Consumer Price Index, which relies on a fixed set of expenditure weights over several years, the PCEPI employs a Fisher Price Index methodology. This approach incorporates expenditure data from both the current and preceding periods. Additionally, the PCEPI uses a chained index, which compares prices from one quarter to the previous quarter rather than anchoring to a fixed base period. This method assumes that consumers adjust their spending patterns in response to changes in relative prices. Historically, the PCEPI has risen approximately one-third of a percent less than the CPI, a trend that has persisted since 1992. An unpublished report by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) attributes much of this discrepancy to differences in the calculation methods for hospital expenses and airfare. In its Monetary Policy Report to the Congress (commonly known as the Humphrey-Hawkins Report) dated February 17, 2000, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announced a shift in its primary measure of inflation. The FOMC transitioned from using the Consumer Price Index to the chain-type price index for personal consumption expenditures as its preferred metric.
